# m22-l03 narration (generated from the outline; do not edit)

## Slide 1

What's Inside an Atom?

Thomson proposed that electrons were spread through a positively charged substance, like raisins in a muffin.

Our big question for this lesson: how were atoms and their structure discovered? By the end of the 1800s, most scientists agreed atoms exist. J.J. Thomson's discovery of the electron showed atoms must be made of even smaller, subatomic particles.

But there were puzzles. Atoms were much more massive than all their electrons put together, so where was the rest of the mass? And atoms are electrically neutral, so how were the negative electrons arranged, and what balanced their charge?

Thomson proposed that the electrons were spread through a positively charged substance, like raisins in a muffin. Then Ernest Rutherford, with his lab partners Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, ran experiments that revealed a very different atom, using equipment like that in Figure 13.

## Slide 3

Rutherford's Investigation.

Alpha particles are massive, positively charged particles that move at high speeds, represented by the symbol alpha.

Rutherford used substances that gave off penetrating rays. Some of these emissions, later named alpha particles, were known to be massive, positively charged, and fast. They're written with the Greek letter alpha. When an alpha particle hit a screen coated with zinc sulfide, it made a tiny flash of light, so the team could see where each one landed.

As Figure 13 shows, Rutherford aimed a beam of alpha particles at an extremely thin sheet of gold foil. He knew Thomson's model, so he expected the massive, speedy alpha particles to pass through the evenly spread positive charge of the gold atoms with only tiny nudges.

## Slide 4

A Shocking Result.

Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, but a few were scattered through very large angles.

The results amazed him. Most of the alpha particles passed through the foil undeflected or barely deflected. But a few scattered through very large angles, and some even bounced back at angles greater than 90 degrees. Figure 14 shows what happened. Only about one in 20,000 was deflected at a large angle.

Rutherford said it was like firing a 15-inch cannon shell at tissue paper and having it bounce back and hit you. He was so surprised because in Thomson's model, nothing inside the atom was concentrated enough to turn a massive, fast-moving alpha particle around.

## Slide 5

The Nuclear Model.

The nucleus is the tiny, massive core of an atom that holds all of its positive charge and more than 99.9 percent of its mass.

Using Coulomb's law and Newton's laws of motion, Rutherford figured out that the results made sense if all the atom's positive charge were packed into a tiny, massive core, now called the nucleus. So his model is called the nuclear model.

We now know the nucleus holds all of an atom's positive charge and more than 99.9 percent of its mass. The electrons add very little mass and are spread through a large volume that stretches far from the nucleus. That volume sets the atom's size, which is about 50,000 times the diameter of the nucleus. An atom is mostly empty space!

## Slide 6

Emission Spectra and Gas-Discharge Tubes.

A gas-discharge tube is a glass tube of low-pressure gas with electrodes at each end that glows when a large potential difference is applied.

How are electrons arranged in the atom? One big clue came from the light atoms give off. As Figure 15 shows, a gas can be made to glow in a gas-discharge tube. Neon signs work the same way.

A gas-discharge tube holds a low-pressure gas in a glass tube with electrodes at each end. Put a large potential difference across it, and the gas glows. What fascinated scientists was that each gas glowed with its own unique color.

## Slide 7

Reading the Fingerprints.

An element's emission spectrum is a unique pattern of bright lines that can be used to identify an unknown sample.

Send the glowing gas's light through a diffraction grating or a prism, and you get an emission spectrum, a fingerprint for each element in the gas. A spectroscope lets you study it in detail. In the diffraction spectroscope in Figure 15, light passes through a slit and then a diffraction grating, which forms an image of the slit at a different position for each wavelength.

A hot glowing solid, like a lightbulb filament, gives a continuous band of colors from red to violet. A gas gives a series of separate colored lines instead. The bottom of Figure 15 shows the bright-line spectra of mercury and neon, and each line is one particular wavelength the gas's atoms emit.

## Slide 8

Identifying Unknown Samples.

The wavelengths in an emission spectrum identify the elements present, and line intensities show their relative concentrations.

Emission spectra make great detective tools. Put an unknown gas in a discharge tube, and the light it emits has a combination of wavelengths unique to its atoms. Compare those wavelengths with the spectra of known gases, and you can identify it.

For a mix of elements, the lines tell you more. Elements present in greater amounts make brighter lines. So the wavelengths tell you which elements are there, and comparing line intensities tells you how much of each. Chemists, engineers, doctors, and environmental scientists use this kind of analysis every day.

## Slide 9

Absorption Spectra.

The absorption spectrum of a gas is the set of wavelengths it absorbs, seen as dark lines in an otherwise continuous spectrum.

Figure 16 shows another identification trick. Shine white light through a gas sample, then through a prism or grating. You get the usual continuous spectrum, but with dark lines where the gas absorbed certain wavelengths. That set of absorbed wavelengths is the gas's absorption spectrum.

Here's the amazing part. For a gas, the bright emission lines and the dark absorption lines fall at exactly the same wavelengths, like sodium's pair of yellow lines at the bottom of Figure 16. Cool gas atoms absorb the very same wavelengths they emit when excited. So the dark lines identify a gas, too.

## Slide 10

Fraunhofer Lines.

Fraunhofer lines are dark lines in the Sun's spectrum caused by gases in its atmosphere absorbing characteristic wavelengths.

In 1814, Josef von Fraunhofer spotted several dark lines in the spectrum of sunlight. These Fraunhofer lines are shown in Figure 17. Later scientists worked out what they meant: as sunlight passes through the gases surrounding the Sun, those gases absorb certain characteristic wavelengths, leaving dark gaps.

Compare the missing lines with the known emission spectra of elements, and you learn what the Sun's atmosphere is made of: mostly hydrogen and helium. Astronomers use the same method on other stars. Starlight's dark absorption lines match the fingerprints of the elements in the star's atmosphere.

## Slide 11

Spectroscopy.

Spectroscopy is the study of spectra, used to analyze, identify, and quantify materials by the light they emit or absorb.

Because every element has its own spectra, scientists can analyze, identify, and measure unknown materials by the light they emit or absorb. That matters in industry, too. Steel mills reprocess huge amounts of scrap iron with all kinds of compositions. Spectrographic analysis reveals a sample's exact makeup in minutes, so the steel can be adjusted to meet specifications.

The study of spectra is called spectroscopy, and spectroscopists work in research and industry. It's a powerful tool for analyzing materials on Earth, and it's the only tool we currently have for finding out what distant stars are made of.

## Slide 12

Hydrogen's Four Visible Lines.

The visible spectrum of hydrogen has four lines: red, green, blue, and violet.

In the 1800s, many physicists studied atomic spectra to figure out the structure of the atom. Hydrogen got lots of attention, because it's the lightest element with the simplest spectrum. Its visible spectrum has four lines, shown in Figure 18: red at 656 nanometers, green at 486, blue at 434, and violet at 410.

Notice the spacing. From red to green is 170 nanometers, from green to blue is 52, and from blue to violet is just 24. As photon energy increases, the lines crowd closer together. Any theory of the atom had to explain these exact wavelengths, and support the nuclear model too.

## Slide 13

Problems with the Planetary Model.

An orbiting electron accelerates, so classical electromagnetism predicts it should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus.

Rutherford had pictured electrons orbiting the nucleus like planets around the Sun. But there was a serious flaw. An orbiting electron is constantly accelerating toward the nucleus, and accelerating electrons radiate electromagnetic waves. At that rate, it would lose energy and spiral into the nucleus in a fraction of a second. But atoms are stable!

The planetary model also predicted that atoms would radiate at all wavelengths. Yet, as you've seen, atoms emit only specific wavelengths.

Danish physicist Niels Bohr went to England in 1911 and soon joined Rutherford's group to work on this puzzle. He tried to combine the nuclear model with Planck's quantized energy and Einstein's theory of light. That was brave, because in 1911 neither idea was widely understood or accepted.

## Slide 14

Stationary States.

A stationary state is a stable orbit in which an electron does not radiate energy, even though it is accelerating.

Bohr started with the planetary arrangement in Figure 19. Then he made a bold proposal: the laws of electromagnetism don't apply inside the atom. An electron in a stable orbit doesn't radiate energy, even though it's accelerating. He called this stable condition a stationary state.

He also assumed each stationary state has its own specific amount of energy. In other words, the energy levels in an atom are quantized.

## Slide 15

Energy Levels Are Like Stairs.

The ground state is an atom's lowest allowed energy, and any energy level above it is an excited state.

Figure 20 compares an atom's energy levels to a staircase with steps that get shorter as you go up. To climb stairs, you go from one step to the next. You can't stop halfway between steps. Electrons have quantized amounts of energy, each called an energy level, and an electron's energy can't fall between allowed levels.

An atom with the smallest allowed energy is in its ground state. When it absorbs energy, one or more electrons jump to higher levels. Any level above the ground state is an excited state. And notice that the energy gap between neighboring levels shrinks as you go higher.

## Slide 16

The Bohr Model.

The Bohr model of the atom is a central nucleus with orbiting electrons that have specific quantized energy levels.

What sets an atom's energy? It's the sum of the electrons' kinetic energy and the potential energy from the attraction between electrons and nucleus. An atom with electrons in a close orbit has less energy than one with electrons far out, because it takes work to pull electrons away from the nucleus. So excited, higher-energy atoms have electrons in bigger, more distant orbits.

Since the energy is quantized and energy is tied to orbit size, the orbit sizes are quantized too. A central nucleus with orbiting electrons at specific quantized energy levels: that's the Bohr model of the atom.

## Slide 17

Emitting Photons.

The energy of an emitted photon equals h f, which equals the decrease in the atom's energy, negative delta E atom.

If stable atoms don't radiate, where do emission spectra come from? Bohr said atoms emit electromagnetic energy when they change from one state to another. Using Einstein's photon theory, he knew every photon's energy is E photon equals h f.

When an atom absorbs a photon, its energy goes up by the photon's energy. When an excited atom drops to a lower level, it emits a photon. Moving from an initial level E i to a final level E f, the atom's energy changes by delta E atom equals E f minus E i. As Figure 21 shows, the emitted photon's energy equals the drop: E photon equals negative delta E atom, which equals E i minus E f.

So the photon's energy is h f, and it equals the decrease in the atom's energy. In Figure 21, the biggest drop, from E three to E one, makes the most energetic photon, with the shortest wavelength.

## Slide 18

Predictions of the Bohr Model.

Bohr's model correctly predicted the wavelengths of light emitted by hydrogen but failed for other elements.

A scientific theory has to do more than make claims. It has to make predictions we can check. A good theory also applies to many problems and gives a simple, unified explanation of part of the world.

Bohr used his theory to calculate the wavelengths of light hydrogen emits, and his numbers matched the measured values beautifully. Because of that, his model was widely accepted.

But it only worked for hydrogen. It couldn't predict the spectrum of helium, the next-simplest element. And nobody had a good explanation for why electromagnetism should work everywhere except inside the atom.

## Slide 19

Building the Model, Forces in the Atom.

Equating Coulomb's force to the electron's mass times centripetal acceleration gives r equals K times the square of e, divided by m times the square of v.

Bohr built his model by applying Newton's second law, F net equals m a, to the electron. The net force is Coulomb's attraction between an electron of charge negative e and a proton of charge positive e, a distance r apart: F equals negative K times the square of e, divided by the square of r.

For an electron circling a much more massive proton, the acceleration is negative the square of v over r, where the negative sign means inward. So Bohr got K times the square of e, over the square of r, equals the electron's mass times the square of v, over r. Solve for r: r equals K times the square of e, divided by the electron's mass times the square of v. Here K, the Coulomb's law constant, is 9.0 times ten to the ninth newton square meters per square coulomb.

## Slide 20

Quantized Angular Momentum.

Bohr postulated that an electron's angular momentum is quantized: m v r equals n h over two pi.

Next Bohr looked at the electron's angular momentum, its momentum times the radius of its orbit, m v r. He proposed that angular momentum is quantized too: it can only be a whole-number multiple of h over two pi, where h is Planck's constant. So the electron's mass times v times r equals n h over two pi.

Solve for v: v equals n h divided by two pi times the electron's mass times r. Put that into the radius equation from before, and Bohr found the allowed orbit radii in hydrogen: r n equals the square of h times the square of n, divided by four times the square of pi, times K, times the electron's mass, times the square of e.

## Slide 21

The Bohr Radius.

The radius of hydrogen's innermost orbit, the Bohr radius, is 5.3 times ten to the negative eleventh meters, or 0.053 nanometers.

Let's find the radius of hydrogen's innermost orbit, called the Bohr radius. Set n equal to 1 and plug in the constants.

The top is the square of 6.63 times ten to the negative thirty-fourth joule seconds, times the square of 1. The bottom is four times the square of pi, times 9.0 times ten to the ninth newton square meters per square coulomb, times 9.11 times ten to the negative thirty-first kilograms, times the square of 1.6 times ten to the negative nineteenth coulombs.

Work it out, and r one equals 5.3 times ten to the negative eleventh meters, or 0.053 nanometers. That's how small hydrogen is!

## Slide 22

The Energy of a Hydrogen Atom.

The energy of a hydrogen atom with principal quantum number n is E n equals negative 13.6 electron volts times one over the square of n.

With a bit more algebra, the atom's total energy, kinetic plus potential, which equals negative K times the square of e over two r, becomes E n equals negative two times the square of pi, times the square of K, times the electron's mass, times e to the fourth power, divided by the square of h, all times one over the square of n. Plugging in the constants gives E n equals negative 2.17 times ten to the negative eighteenth joules times one over the square of n. In electron volts, using 1 electron volt equals 1.6 times ten to the negative nineteenth joules, E n equals negative 13.6 electron volts times one over the square of n.

So energy is quantized too. The whole number n in both the radius and energy equations is called the principal quantum number, and it sets the allowed values of r and E.

Figure 22 shows the first four. The radius grows as the square of n: 5.3 times ten to the negative eleventh meters, then 2.1 times ten to the negative tenth, 4.8 times ten to the negative tenth, and 8.5 times ten to the negative tenth meters. The energy goes as one over the square of n: negative 13.6, negative 3.4, negative 1.51, and negative 0.85 electron volts, creeping toward zero. Bigger orbit, smaller energy magnitude.

## Slide 23

Why Negative Energy? Transitions.

Zero energy is defined as an electron infinitely far from the nucleus with no kinetic energy, so a bound atom has negative total energy.

Why is the atom's energy negative? Only energy differences affect motion, so we can pick zero anywhere. Here, zero is the energy when the electron is infinitely far from the nucleus with no kinetic energy, the condition of an ionized atom with its electron removed. It takes work to ionize an atom, so an atom holding an electron has less than zero energy. Jumping to a higher level makes the energy less negative, a positive change.

Figure 23 shows hydrogen's levels and possible transitions. An excited hydrogen atom can emit infrared, visible, or ultraviolet light, depending on the jump. Dropping to the ground state from any excited state gives ultraviolet light, the Lyman series. Dropping to n equals 3 gives infrared, the Paschen series. And hydrogen's four visible lines, the Balmer series, come from drops into n equals 2 from n equals 3, 4, 5, and 6.

## Slide 24

Example Problem 4, Energy Levels.

The energy an atom absorbs is delta E equals E f minus E i.

To move a hydrogen electron from the lowest level, n equals 1, to the second, n equals 2, the atom must absorb energy. Find the energies of both levels and the energy absorbed.

Step one: analyze and sketch. Diagram levels E one and E two, and show which way energy increases. Known: n equals 1 for the innermost level and n equals 2 for the second. Unknown: E one, E two, and delta E.

Step two: solve. Use E n equals negative 13.6 electron volts times one over the square of n. For n equals 1, E one is negative 13.6 electron volts. For n equals 2, E two is negative 13.6 times one fourth, or negative 3.40 electron volts. The energy absorbed is the final level minus the initial level: E two minus E one, negative 3.40 electron volts minus negative 13.6 electron volts, which is 10.2 electron volts. Energy is absorbed.

Step three: evaluate. Orbital energies are in electron volts. The difference is positive, as it should be moving up. And about 10 electron volts is the size we expect for this jump.

## Slide 25

Example Problem 5, Emitted Photons.

The wavelength of an emitted photon is lambda equals h c over delta E.

An excited hydrogen electron drops from n equals 2 to n equals 1. Find the energy and wavelength of the emitted photon, using the levels from Example Problem 4.

Step one: analyze and sketch. Diagram E one and E two, show the direction of increasing energy, and draw the emitted photon. Known: E one is negative 13.6 electron volts and E two is negative 3.40 electron volts. Unknown: delta E, the frequency, and the wavelength.

Step two: solve. The photon's energy is negative delta E, the drop from the initial level to the final level: E i minus E f, which is E two minus E one, negative 3.40 electron volts minus negative 13.6 electron volts, or 10.2 electron volts. Energy is emitted. For the wavelength, delta E equals h f, so f equals delta E over h. And c equals lambda f, so lambda equals c over f. Substitute f, and lambda equals h c over delta E: 1240 electron volt nanometers divided by 10.2 electron volts, which is 122 nanometers.

Step three: evaluate. Energy is in electron volts and wavelength in nanometers, a version of the meter. The atom releases energy, so its energy change is negative. And 122 nanometers is below 400 nanometers, in the ultraviolet, just right for a drop to the ground state.

## Slide 26

Bohr's Legacy.

The ionization energy of an atom is the energy needed to completely free an electron from the atom.

The Bohr model can't correctly predict electron energies for atoms with many electrons. Even so, it was a huge step forward. Bohr and his students also calculated hydrogen's ionization energy, the energy needed to completely free an electron from the atom, and it closely matched experiments.

The model also helped explain some chemical properties of the elements. It led to the idea that each element has a unique arrangement of electrons, which is the foundation of much of what we know about chemical reactions and bonding. Niels Bohr won the Nobel Prize in 1922 for his work on understanding the atom.
